blogs.title: When the Second DuPont Factor Wins: Why Apex Bank’s Services Are ‘Legally Identical’ to Credit‑Card Services
blogs.description: This post will dissect the Court’s treatment of the second DuPont factor, explaining how the Board’s statutory definition of credit‑card services dovetails with the broader legal meanings of banking and financing. We’ll explore the implications for other institutions that offer “financial services” under a single brand, and assess whether Apex’s insistence on separating credit‑card offerings from core banking services overlooks the evolving landscape of fintech and digital‑only banks.

blogs.title: The Sixth DuPont Factor Re‑opened: A Window of Opportunity for Trademark Registrants in a Crowded Field
blogs.description: Here we focus on the Court’s vacatur of the sixth factor, outlining the standard for ‘similar goods’ when the services are already deemed highly similar under the second factor. The analysis will chart how a broader universe of third‑party marks can shift the commercial‑strength calculus and ultimately alter the scope of protection for inherently distinctive marks like CC Serve’s ‘ASPIRE.’

blogs.title: Commercial Impression vs. Commercial Strength: Why the First DuPont Factor Matters Even When the Second Factor Is Decisive
blogs.description: This entry will explore the Court’s reasoning that a vacated sixth‑factor analysis can affect the overall commercial impression, necessitating a new look at the first factor. The post will discuss how courts tease apart appearance, sound, and connotation, what this means for word‑and‑design marks, and whether Apex’s proposed ‘ASPIRE BANK’ could survive once the Board’s view of the mark’s distinctiveness changes.

blogs.title: The Future of Internet‑Only Banking Trademarks: Lessons from Apex Bank v. CC Serve for New FinTech Entrants
blogs.description: A forward‑looking piece that looks beyond the direct parties, focusing on the broader trend of digital‑only banks using legacy financial trademarks. We’ll evaluate how the Court’s decisions—especially the vacated sixth factor—inform the risk calculus for future entrants that wish to piggyback on familiar marks, and what tactics (e.g., distinct design elements, new service classes) may mitigate likelihood‑of‑confusion challenges.
